1.pericope_label: Ziba meets the fleeing king with provisions, slanders Mephibosheth, and is granted his master’s lands

schools.summary: Henry reads Ziba as a man not content to be manager but longing to be master of the estate, fishing in troubled waters, since a grant from the crown would serve him whichever side prevailed; the present was timed to incline the king towards him, a man’s gift making room for him before great men. On the apportioning he takes the allocation literally and makes a point of the wine, designed for such as were faint and not for the king or his courtiers: blessed is the land whose princes use wine for strength, as David did, and not for drunkenness, as Absalom did. On the judgment he is severest with David, who knew the man was not ambitious but easy in his place, nor could expect with his lame legs to climb the ladder of preferment, yet credited the calumny and without further enquiry convicted him of treason and granted away his lands — a rash judgment of which he was afterwards ashamed.

Gill is the most measured on the forfeiture: had the charge been true the sentence would have been righteous, the lands having been forfeited once already by Ishbosheth’s rebellion and then graciously restored, yet it seems too hasty a step to give them away without further inquiry into the truth of the accusation.

Ellicott holds that Ziba grossly slandered his master, doubtless for personal gain, and draws a harder inference still, that a man showing so entire a want of principle can have adhered to David’s cause only because he had the shrewdness to foresee its ultimate success. He calls the story as told against Mephibosheth almost too improbable to be believed, since a helpless cripple of Saul’s house could hardly have hoped the rebellion would bring him the throne; but David, apt to be hasty in his judgments, was in a state to believe any tale of ingratitude and was deeply affected by so large a contribution to his necessities. Keil and Delitzsch put the motive plainly as calumny in the hope of getting possession of the lands he was farming for his master, add that Mephibosheth had never put in any claim to the throne before, and conclude that in the excited state he was then in the king was weak enough to credit the charge and commit the injustice. They take the apportioning of the present literally, the asses for the king’s family to ride in turn, the bread and fruit for the servants and the wine for such as should faint in the desert, and treat the written form of one word in the verse as a copyist’s error.

Clarke does not argue the motive but exclaims against it, asking what a base wretch this was and how unfounded the accusation against a peaceable and innocent man. His chief work is on the present itself: the word loaf gives a false idea of ancient Jewish bread, which was thin cakes and not yeasted and raised like ours; the summer fruits were probably cucumbers or watermelons, used in those countries to refresh travellers in the burning heat, which Harmer supposes to be why they bear that name; and the bottle was a goat’s skin, the general vessel of the East. On the apportioning he reads a formula rather than a plan, this being the Eastern manner of speaking when anything is presented to a great man, that this and this is for the slaves of the servants of your majesty, when the presents are intended for the sovereign himself and are so understood — a compliment amounting to the claim that they are not worthy of his acceptance. Wesley adds only that the bottle was a large one, proportionable to the rest of the provisions.

debates.question: Is the itemising of the present a literal allocation or an Eastern form of compliment?

positions.view: A set form of speech, the gift being meant for the sovereign himself and so understood
A literal allocation — asses to ride, bread and fruit for the servants, wine for the faint

debates.question: Why did David credit the charge without enquiry?

positions.view: Apt to be hasty in his judgments, ready to believe any tale of ingratitude, and moved by the size of the gift
Weak enough in the excited state he was then in to credit it and commit the injustice
A rash judgment of which he was afterwards ashamed, since he knew the man was not ambitious

outliers.claim: Alone in inferring from Ziba’s want of principle that he had followed David only because he foresaw David would win.
Alone in correcting the English of the gift — the loaf, the summer fruits and the bottle — rather than weighing the motive.
Alone in allowing that the forfeiture would have been righteous had the charge been true, the lands having been forfeited once before.

themes: thine are all that pertained unto Mephibosheth
wine, that such as be faint in the wilderness may drink

5.pericope_label: Shimei of the house of Saul curses and stones the king, and David forbids Abishai to kill him

schools.summary: Henry sets this scene against the one before it: David bore Shimei’s curses much better than he had borne Ziba’s flatteries, since by the flatteries he was brought to pass a wrong judgment on another and by the curses to pass a right judgment on himself — the world’s smiles being more dangerous than its frowns. He gives reasons why this moment was chosen, that it now seemed safe, though it would have cost the man his life had the king resented it, and that David’s distress seemed to make Providence endorse the reproach, which was the principle on which Job’s friends condemned him. He notes that the dust thrown would blow back into the thrower’s own eyes, as causeless curses return upon their author’s head. On the hard saying he distinguishes the act from the affliction: as Shimei’s sin it was not from God but from his own wicked heart, and God’s hand in it neither excused nor extenuated it, any more than it did the sin of those who put Christ to death; but as David’s affliction it was from the Lord. He alone supplies the mechanism, that of Saul’s blood David’s conscience acquitted him but it charged him with the blood of Uriah, so that the reproach was too true, though false as Shimei meant it.

Gill calls the insinuations false, as if David had stirred up the Philistines to the battle in which Saul fell, and he notices that the giving up of Saul’s seven descendants, though related later in the book, seems to have happened before this. On the rebuff of Abishai he supposes Joab to have joined his brother and offers a choice of senses for the formula — either a refusal of their counsel, or the question what is it to me or to you, since the cursing will hurt neither of us.

Keil and Delitzsch say outright that what blood is meant cannot be determined with certainty, and allow that Shimei may have laid the deaths of Ishbosheth and Abner to David’s charge, innocent though he was of both. They take the formula about the sons of Zeruiah to signify that a man wished nothing in common with another’s feelings and views, and suppose Joab to have joined his brother in the request. On the hard saying they work on the text, holding the written form to mean upon the guilt that really belongs to me, and denying that the word in question ever means misery. Ellicott doubts whether more was meant by the charge than holding David responsible generally for the blood of Saul’s house, instancing those same deaths and the execution of Saul’s seven descendants at the Gibeonites’ demand, and he too places that execution before this flight. On the hard saying he works on David’s intention, holding that the king does not justify the wrong done him, but that so far as it bears upon himself it is of divine appointment and therefore not to be resented.

Clarke works on the particle, which he would render not because but for if — for if the Lord hath said unto him, Curse David, who shall then say, Wherefore hast thou done so? He adds that no soul of man can suppose God ever bade one man curse another, this being a peculiarity of the Hebrew language, which does not always distinguish between permission and commandment. Wesley works on providence instead: God put no wickedness into Shimei’s heart, which was of itself full of malignity, but left him to it and brought David so low that he might seem a proper object of scorn, which is ground enough for an expression that speaks not by the word of his precept but by the word of his providence. Wesley also gives the formula about the sons of Zeruiah flatly as a refusal of counsel, in this matter I ask not your advice, nor will I follow it, and offers the same alternatives as the others for the blood charged.

debates.question: What blood of the house of Saul is laid to David’s charge?

positions.view: It cannot be determined with certainty; perhaps the deaths of Ishbosheth and Abner
Probably no more than a general responsibility for the blood of Saul’s house, including the seven descendants given to the Gibeonites
A false insinuation, as if David had stirred up the Philistines to the battle in which Saul fell

debates.question: In what sense had the Lord said to Shimei, Curse David?

positions.view: The particle should be read for if, and the Hebrew does not always distinguish permission from commandment
By the word of his providence and not of his precept, God leaving Shimei to his own malignity
David neither justifies the wrong nor resents it, taking it as of divine appointment so far as it bears on himself
Shimei’s sin was from his own heart and not excused by God’s hand in it; David’s affliction was from the Lord

debates.question: What does the formula about the sons of Zeruiah mean?

positions.view: That a man wished nothing in common with another’s feelings and views
Either a refusal of their counsel, or that the cursing will hurt neither of us
Flatly a refusal of counsel — in this matter I ask not your advice

outliers.claim: Alone in reading David’s conscience as acquitting him of Saul’s blood but charging him with Uriah’s, so that the reproach was true though falsely meant.
Alone in observing that the thrown dust would blow back into the thrower’s own eyes.
Alone in resting the hard saying on the rendering of a single Hebrew particle.

what have I to do with you, ye sons of Zeruiah
the LORD hath said unto him, Curse David
it may be that the LORD will look on mine affliction

15.pericope_label: Hushai makes his way into Absalom’s confidence, and Ahithophel counsels the taking of his father’s concubines

schools.summary: Henry frames the two counsellors as a single ruin. Absalom thought himself sure of success in having the two most celebrated politicians of the age, relying upon them and not consulting the ark, though he had it with him; yet miserable counsellors were they both, the one an enemy who would never counsel him to do wisely, the other counselling him to do wickedly and so betraying him as effectually as the man who meant to. A government founded in sin, he concludes, is founded upon the sand. He observes further that the greatest politicians often act most foolishly for themselves, this one being cried up as an oracle and yet throwing in with a rash youth whose fall he of all men might have foreseen. He also reports, as what some think, the private motive that Ahithophel acted to revenge the injury done to Bathsheba.

Gill has Absalom put the question to Hushai not in displeasure but overjoyed that so trusty a friend of his father’s had deserted him, and only to try the man’s integrity. He notices how the question is worded, that Absalom will not name David, nor give him his title, nor own the relation of a father, but says merely thy friend, and that he could not charge ingratitude without reproaching himself. On the roof he says the deed was done upon the very spot from which David had the sight of Bathsheba.

Keil and Delitzsch call Hushai’s opening declaration that Jehovah had chosen Absalom great craftiness, adding that he could at least come to no other conclusion judging from the results. They call Ahithophel’s advice sagacious enough, since to take the royal harem was to appropriate the throne, making reconciliation with David impossible and so binding Absalom’s followers the more firmly to his cause; and they close with the historian’s own estimate, that this counsel was in those days with both father and son as if a man had enquired of the word of God. Ellicott reads the question to Hushai as surprise rather than pleasure, Absalom being inclined to distrust a man who had deserted his master, and reads the answer as argument rather than trick, Hushai resting his conduct on loyalty to the government in fact, urging that this has divine authority, and offering his past faithfulness as a pledge of faithfulness now. On the harem he remarks that taking a predecessor’s wives was an Oriental custom to whose enormity the mind was blunted by polygamy; and on the roof he observes that Nathan had foretold that the public punishment should answer to the secret crime, finding it striking that it fell on the very roof where David had first yielded.

Clarke names the answer an equivocation: Hushai meant in his heart that God and Israel had chosen David, but spoke so as to make Absalom believe he spoke of him — and whatever insincerity appears in it, Hushai is alone answerable. On the counsel he calls the measure infernal, notes that a conquered king’s wives were always the property of the conqueror and that Herodotus reports Smerdis espousing all his predecessor’s, but insists that for a son to take his father’s was the sum of abomination and death by the law, rarely found even among the Gentiles; and he thinks the deed was done upon the very spot where David’s eye had taken its adulterous view. Wesley agrees that the question was put only to try Hushai, and reads its wording as a reflection upon David, a friend to strangers but not to his own son, whom by his severity he had provoked, so that Absalom does not vouchsafe to call him his father. Wesley also supplies the private motive plainly, that Ahithophel acted partly to revenge the injury done to Bathsheba, the daughter of his own son.

debates.question: How should Absalom’s question to Hushai be heard?

positions.view: Not in displeasure but overjoyed, and put only to try the man’s integrity
As surprise, Absalom being inclined to distrust a man who had deserted his master

debates.question: What is Hushai’s profession of loyalty to Absalom?

positions.view: Great craftiness, though judging from the results he could come to no other conclusion
An argument rather than a trick, resting on loyalty to the government in fact and its divine authority
An equivocation, meant in his heart of David; whatever insincerity appears in it, Hushai alone is answerable

debates.question: What moved Ahithophel to give this counsel?

positions.view: Sound policy — to appropriate the throne, make reconciliation impossible, and bind Absalom’s followers to him
Partly revenge for the injury done to Bathsheba, the daughter of his own son

outliers.claim: Alone in absolving David of the equivocation and laying the whole insincerity on Hushai’s own account.
Alone in making the two counsellors one ruin and in drawing from it that a government founded in sin is founded on sand.
Alone in excusing the custom, the mind having been blunted by polygamy to the enormity of taking a predecessor’s harem.

themes: is this thy kindness to thy friend
go in unto thy father’s concubines
the counsel of Ahithophel was as if a man had enquired at the oracle of God
